name: Cosmelan peel

lead: Cosmelan is a professional depigmenting treatment from the Spanish company mesoestetic, marketed for melasma, post-inflammatory marks, sun spots and freckles. People use it to fade dark patches and even out skin tone.

It has two phases: a mask applied in clinic and left on for several hours, then roughly six months of home cream and sun protection. The company says it corrects existing spots and regulates melanin production, and that it suits all skin types. These are manufacturer claims, and no peer-reviewed trials were found.

paras: The mask goes on in a clinic visit, then a home cream is used daily for months alongside strict sunscreen. Redness and peeling in the first days are typical, and fading builds across the home-care phase.

The company discusses irritation and rebound pigmentation, and stresses sun protection to avoid it. Contraindications listed by the maker include pregnancy, isotretinoin use and a history of vitiligo.

angle.text: People use Cosmelan to fade melasma and dark spots into a more even tone. The mask and months of home cream aim to reduce melanin production so patches lighten. Claims come from the manufacturer, and no published trials were found.

lead: Cosmelan is a professional depigmenting treatment from the Spanish company mesoestetic, used to even out facial skin tone by lightening melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, sun spots (solar lentigines) and freckles. People seek it for a clearer, more uniform complexion when dark patches dominate how the face looks [1].

According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference drawing on company material, the treatment has two phases: an in-clinic mask applied by a trained professional and left on for several hours, followed by about six months of home cream and sun protection [1]. The company says it corrects existing spots and regulates melanin production, and that it suits all phototypes; these are manufacturer claims [1].

Melasma itself is a chronic, relapsing condition for which dermatology references list topical agents such as hydroquinone, azelaic acid and kojic acid, oral tranexamic acid, chemical peels and lasers, with strict sun protection described as essential [2]. No peer-reviewed trials of Cosmelan were found.
infobox: In-clinic mask, then about 6 months of home cream

sections.h: Protocol as described by the manufacturer
paras: A trained professional applies the Cosmelan 1 mask to the face, left on for a period set by severity (described as 6 to 8 hours), and the patient later starts a Cosmelan 2 cream regimen about a week after mask removal, supported by a soothing barrier balm and high-SPF sunscreen. The company says the protocol was revised around 2024 to shorten mask exposure and delay the home phase, and that treatment must be done through authorized centers [1].

Melasma causes tan, brown or gray patches, usually on the face. Its cause is thought to involve sun exposure, hormonal influences, genetics and skin irritation, and it is more common in women and in people with darker skin types and sunny climates [2]. It is chronic and relapsing, and even small amounts of sun can bring faded patches back [2].

Treatments listed include hydroquinone, tretinoin, azelaic acid, cysteamine, kojic acid, alpha arbutin, oral tranexamic acid, chemical peels, microdermabrasion and lasers; combination creams tend to work better than single agents, and treatments can cause irritation, lighter patches or contact dermatitis [2]. Chemical peels in general range from mild alpha hydroxy acid peels to deep phenol-based peels, with deeper peels carrying more risk of complications such as prolonged redness and pigmentary changes [3].

The manufacturer's consent form lists pregnancy and breastfeeding, product hypersensitivity, current oral isotretinoin, active infection, a history of hypopigmentation such as vitiligo, and open wounds as contraindications, with caution for a history of herpes simplex or keloids [1].
No studies found. The company cites more than one million treatments worldwide, which is a usage figure rather than a study [1].
